name: New Jersey Dutch Gambrel

revival_periods.note: This is the variant the revival actually copied — and immediately falsified, by replacing the sprung eave with a straight overhang and cutting a full-width shed dormer into the roof.

regions: Passaic and Hudson counties, New Jersey
Somerset and Middlesex counties, New Jersey
geography.hearth: the Hackensack and Passaic valleys of Bergen County, on the red sandstone of the Newark Basin

lineage.note: The Bergen population was heavily Flemish and Walloon, and the sprung eave has better parallels in the southern Low Countries than in Holland proper.

description.short: The Bergen County sandstone house: a low gambrel-roofed block whose lower roof slope sweeps out past the wall on a concave curve, shading the front and eventually becoming a porch.
description.long:
This is a house made of one geological accident and one roof idea. The accident is the Newark Basin sandstone — a red-brown stone that quarries in beds, dresses easily, and lies directly under the Hackensack and Passaic valleys. Bergen builders used it for everything, and used it with a very particular economy: dressed, squared and coursed on the entrance elevation, coursed rubble on the two ends, and whatever came out of the ground on the back. Walk around one of these houses and the quality of the masonry degrades with each turn. That is not carelessness; it is an exact allocation of skilled labour to the surface that will be seen.

The roof idea is the gambrel with a sprung eave, and it deserves careful description because almost everything built in its name since 1890 has got it wrong. A Bergen gambrel has a steep lower slope, sixty to seventy-two degrees, and a shallow upper one, eighteen to thirty degrees, which converts a low masonry wall into a full upper storey without building the wall any higher — an enormous economy when the wall is two feet of hand-laid stone. Then the lower slope does not stop at the wall. It continues past it on a concave sweep, projecting eighteen to thirty-six inches, flattening as it goes, so that the eave line is a curve rather than an angle. This throws rain clear of an unrendered stone wall and puts the summer sun off the openings entirely. In the middle of the eighteenth century somebody put posts under the sprung eave and extended it to eight or ten feet, and the full-width Dutch porch was born — the direct ancestor of a habit that would eventually cover the entire United States.

The plan behind it stays simple and stays Dutch for a long time: one or two rooms deep, gable-end chimneys, no passage, low ceilings at seven and a half to eight and a half feet, a Dutch door with a transom, and after about 1760 a five-bay front with the door in the middle because the neighbours were English. The interior keeps anchor beams and, on early work, jambless hearths.

What it feels like is low, broad and sheltering — the opposite of the Hudson Valley house's vertical roof. You approach across a shaded band of ground under the sprung eave; the wall is warm red stone with white mortar; and the roof, which is most of what you see, curves down to meet you at head height and then stops. The Colonial Revival spent forty years trying to reproduce that feeling with a shed dormer and a straight soffit, and never once managed it, because the curve was the whole thing.

defining_characteristics: Gambrel roof with a steep lower slope (60–72 degrees) and a shallow upper slope (18–30 degrees), the break at 55–70% of the half-span
A sprung (flared) eave: the lower slope continues past the wall face on a concave sweep, projecting 18–36 in, later carried on posts as a full-width porch
Load-bearing red-brown Newark Basin sandstone, dressed and coursed on the entrance elevation only, rubble elsewhere
Low wall: plate 7 ft 6 in – 9 ft 0 in above the floor, so the gambrel does the work a second storey would otherwise do
Chimneys at the gable ends, one or both, serving hearths in each principal room
Three- or five-bay eave-front elevation with a Dutch door, transom-lit after c. 1760
No dormers on the original front slope
diagnostic_tells: The eave is a curve, not an angle — sight along the roof edge and the concave sweep is unmistakable
Masonry quality drops with each elevation as you walk around the house
Gambrel with no dormer at all; if there is a continuous dormer the building postdates 1890
Red-brown stone with wide white lime joints, laid in courses of unequal height
The porch, where present, is an extension of the roof plane rather than a separate structure with its own pitch

distinguished_from.difference: The most instructive pairing in the whole Dutch branch. The revival keeps the gambrel and discards everything that made it work: it cuts a full-width shed dormer into the front slope (which no colonial Jersey Dutch house has), replaces the concave sprung eave with a straight overhanging soffit, frames in wood with a veneer or shingle skin, and imposes symmetry on every elevation. Test the eave profile and the dormer; either one settles it.
Steep straight gable versus gambrel; grey limestone versus red sandstone; a water-shedding sprung eave of 18–24 in versus a sheltering one of 24–36 in that becomes a porch.

Both are Mid-Atlantic stone houses with five-bay fronts after 1760. The Georgian house has a centre passage, aligned windows on all elevations, a classical door surround and a gable roof at 8:12–10:12; the Jersey Dutch house has a gambrel, a sprung eave, no passage and a plain door under a transom.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The gambrel geometry: the break point is chosen so that the upper floor gains full headroom at the knee wall without raising the masonry.
typical_ratios: Overall 30–46 ft × 22–30 ft; one or two rooms deep
Lower slope 60–72 degrees; upper slope 18–30 degrees; break at 55–70% of the half-span
Plate 7 ft 6 in – 9 ft 0 in; ridge 20–24 ft above grade
Sprung eave projection 24–36 in, sweep radius 4–8 ft; posted porch 8–10 ft deep
Wall thickness 20–28 in; ceiling 7 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three bays early, five after c. 1760, with the door centred once symmetry arrives; window widths equal and piers wider than the openings.

massing_affinities.note: The plan under the gambrel before Anglicization.
The post-1760 Bergen house with a centre hall behind a Dutch section.
Growth by adding a kitchen wing along the ridge line.

constraints.statement: Gambrel geometry: lower slope 60–72 degrees, upper slope 18–30 degrees, break at 55–70% of the half-span. The two slopes must differ by at least 30 degrees or the roof reads as a modern barn profile.

test.note: This variant states the differentiation itself as the enforceable rule ('must differ by at least 30 degrees'), unlike the parent dutch-colonial-american's softer version -- so the difference expression is the more faithful test here, not the raw range.

constraints.statement: The eave must spring — a concave sweep projecting 24–36 in beyond the wall face, with a sweep radius of 4–8 ft. A straight overhang of any depth is not this type.

test.note: The sweep radius (4-8ft) is the same statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No continuous shed dormer on any roof slope. This is the diagnostic marker of Dutch Colonial Revival and is absent from every colonial Bergen house.

Dressed and coursed sandstone confined to the entrance elevation; coursed rubble at the ends; random rubble at the rear. Uniform ashlar on all four sides is a later or wealthier building and reads as such.
Where the sprung eave is posted to form a porch, depth 8–10 ft with posts 8–10 ft on centre; the porch roof is the continued roof plane, not a separate structure with its own pitch.

test.note: A posted porch under the sprung eave is the same depth concept as a galerie/piazza.

exemplars.name: Steuben House (Zabriskie House)
exemplars.location: Historic New Bridge Landing, River Edge, New Jersey
exemplars.note: Kinderkamack Ridge sandstone, dressed on the two road-facing sides and coursed rubble elsewhere; enlarged c. 1765 when the fashionable gambrel roof was added.

exemplars.name: Hopper-Goetschius House
exemplars.location: 363 East Saddle River Road, Upper Saddle River, New Jersey
exemplars.note: Listed on the National Register within the Early Stone Houses of Bergen County multiple property submission — the single best documentary group for this variant.

exemplars.name: Dyckman Farmhouse
exemplars.note: Just outside New Jersey but structurally of this family: fieldstone below, frame above, gambrel with a sprung eave carried on posts.

proportion_packs.note: The type this pack was written from, and the node that supplies most of its numbers: the lower slope at 60-72 degrees, the upper at 18-30, the break at 55-70 percent of the half-span, the plate at 7 ft 6 in to 9 ft, the sweep at a 4-8 ft radius projecting 24-36 in, and the ridge 20-24 ft above grade. Bound primary because on this node the roof IS the design -- this record's own governing_logic says so in one sentence, 'the gambrel geometry: the break point is chosen so that the upper floor gains full headroom at the knee wall without raising the masonry', which is a statement that the section generates the building. timber-bay stays and is not displaced: it owns the H-bent frame bay, this pack owns the roof, and the one place they meet -- the house depth, which is the bent span and also the roof's generator -- is flagged in this pack's own depth rule as two constraints that are usually discussed separately and are the same constraint.

Bound on inheritance from the parent dutch-colonial-american rather than on this variant's own text, which foregrounds the gambrel roof geometry (the break point set so the upper floor gains full headroom without raising the masonry) rather than the framing bay as its stated governing_logic — no pack among the 36 models gambrel break-point geometry or the curvature of a sprung eave, and that gap is reported rather than papered over. The plan module this variant records — 22-30 ft deep, one or two rooms — is consistent with the wider Dutch H-bent bay rhythm, but new-jersey-dutch-gambrel is not itself named in timber-bay's own applies_to (unlike the parent and the Hudson Valley variant), so this binding is an extension of the family's logic rather than a separately attested one.

new-jersey-dutch-gambrel is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. One or two rooms deep, gable-end chimneys, no passage until Anglicization — the plan is constrained by span, hearth and daylight exactly as the pack describes, not proportioned by ratio.

Unlike its Hudson Valley sibling, this variant's own proportional_system already classifies its symmetry as 'near-symmetrical' rather than 'additive-vernacular,' and states plainly that the door centres 'once symmetry arrives' after c. 1760 on a five-bay front — which covers most of the variant's later floruit (1730-1820). Bound at facade role rather than merely optional for that reason, while still noting the pack's odd-bay/single-entrance model describes only the post-1760 Anglicized form; earlier Bergen sandstone houses (e.g. the Steuben House's 1752 core) are three-bay and not yet composed to this discipline. brick-course was considered and rejected: the style's own diagnostic tells state the stone is 'laid in courses of unequal height,' which contradicts the pack's core premise of a fixed mason's-gauge-rod coursing, unlike the tighter-coursed Hudson Valley sibling.
